title: Snapshot Array
description:
Design an integer array that can be snapshotted, where any element can later be read as it was at any past snapshot.

- `SnapshotArray(length)` creates an array of the given length with every element equal to `0`.
- `set(index, val)` sets the element at `index` to `val`.
- `snap()` takes a snapshot and returns its id. Ids start at `0` and increase by one with every call.
- `get(index, snap_id)` returns the value at `index` as it was right after snapshot `snap_id` was taken.

The array can be long and snapshots frequent, so copying the whole array on every `snap` is too slow.

examples.explanation: Snapshot 0 was taken while index 0 held 5. Setting it to 6 afterwards does not change what snapshot 0 recorded.
Elements that were never set read as 0 in every snapshot.

hints: Most elements do not change between snapshots, so store changes, not copies.
For each index keep a list of (snap_id, value) pairs recording when the value changed. The list is sorted by snap_id automatically.
On get, binary search that index's list for the last pair with snap_id <= the requested id. If set is called twice in the same snapshot period, overwrite the last pair instead of appending.
approach:
**Key insight: persist the diffs, not the array.** Each index keeps its own change log: a list of `(snap_id, value)` pairs where `snap_id` is the id the *next* `snap()` call will return, i.e. the snapshot that will first observe this value. Because the current snap id only grows, every log is sorted, and `get` is a binary search for the last pair whose id is <= the requested snapshot.

Seeding every log with `(0, 0)` means an element that was never set reads as 0 at every snapshot, and the search always finds something. If `set` is called repeatedly between two snaps, only the latest value can ever be observed, so overwrite the last pair instead of appending; this bounds the log by the number of snaps plus one.

`snap()` is O(1): it just bumps a counter. Nothing is copied.

**Common mistakes:** copying the array in `snap` (O(length) per snap, times out); storing the snap id that was *last* taken instead of the one that will be taken next, which is off by one; using `bisect_left`, which misses an exact match on the snap id.

**Interview follow-ups:** This is the simplest persistent data structure; compare with a persistent segment tree or copy-on-write pages used by databases and filesystems (ZFS, Btrfs) and by MVCC. Memory: logs grow with the number of distinct writes, so a long-lived system needs snapshot retirement (drop pairs older than the oldest live snapshot). Concurrency: `snap` must be atomic with respect to `set` so a snapshot sees a consistent state; a reader-writer lock or a per-snapshot epoch works.

complexity.time: O(1) set and snap, O(log s) get where s is the number of changes to that index
